questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: What is the total testing time of the Digital SAT (excluding the break)?
questions.e: The Digital SAT is 2 hours 14 minutes (134 minutes): 64 minutes for Reading & Writing and 70 minutes for Math.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Each Digital SAT section is scored on what scale?
questions.e: Each section (Reading & Writing, Math) is scored 200–800, for a total score of 400–1600.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: How many questions are in the Reading & Writing section?
questions.e: Reading & Writing has 54 questions across two 32-minute modules (27 questions each).

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: How many questions are in the Math section?
questions.e: Math has 44 questions across two 35-minute modules (22 questions each).

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The Digital SAT adapts at which level?
o: It does not adapt at all
questions.e: The SAT uses multistage adaptive testing: Module 1 performance determines whether Module 2 is the harder or easier version.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: What happens if you answer a question incorrectly on the Digital SAT?
o: Nothing — wrong answers score the same as blanks
questions.e: There is no guessing penalty: wrong answers and blanks both earn zero. Always answer every question.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which app delivers the Digital SAT on test day?
questions.e: The Digital SAT is taken in the College Board's Bluebook testing app, which you must download before test day.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The built-in Desmos graphing calculator is available on:
questions.e: Desmos is built into Bluebook and available on all Math questions; you may also bring an approved personal calculator.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The standard SAT registration fee for U.S. test takers is:
questions.e: The base registration fee is $68 (2026 cycle). International test takers add a $43 international fee, for $111 total.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: For international test takers, the total SAT registration cost is typically:
questions.e: $68 base + $43 international registration fee = $111 (a $24 test-center fee can apply at some centers).

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: How long is the break between the two Digital SAT sections?
questions.e: There is a single 10-minute break between the Reading & Writing and Math sections.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Each Reading & Writing module lasts:
questions.e: Each R&W module is 32 minutes with 27 questions — about 1 minute 11 seconds per question.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Each Math module lasts:
questions.e: Each Math module is 35 minutes with 22 questions — about 1 minute 35 seconds per question.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Reading & Writing passages on the Digital SAT are:
questions.e: The digital format replaced long passages with short 25–150-word texts, each paired with exactly one question.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: To earn the highest possible scores, a student generally needs:
o: The easier Module 2 in both sections
The harder Module 2 in both sections
questions.e: The harder Module 2 contains the questions that unlock the top of the 200–800 scale; the easier Module 2 caps the section score.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Total scores on the Digital SAT are reported:
questions.e: Scores are reported in 10-point increments (e.g., 1250, 1260) — there are no scores like 1253.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which of these is NOT tested on the Digital SAT?
questions.e: The SAT essay was discontinued; the digital test has only Reading & Writing and Math sections.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Students can send their SAT scores to how many colleges for free?
o: Four, if designated within 9 days of the test
questions.e: Four score reports are free if recipients are designated before or within 9 days after the test; additional reports cost $15 each.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Late registration for the SAT adds approximately:
questions.e: Late registration adds a $38 fee on top of the standard registration fee (always confirm current fees on collegeboard.org).

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: What should a student do with seconds remaining and unanswered questions?
o: Leave them blank to avoid a penalty
questions.e: With no guessing penalty, an unanswered question is a guaranteed zero — a guess has a 25%+ chance of being right.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The Math section includes which question formats?
questions.e: Math mixes multiple-choice questions with student-produced responses (grid-ins) where you type your own answer.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which statement about Module 2 routing is true?
o: It is based on how fast you finish Module 1
It is based on Module 1 accuracy
questions.e: Bluebook scores Module 1 and routes you based on accuracy — not speed, and not by choice.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Scores for the Digital SAT are typically released:
questions.e: Digital SAT scores are released online in about 2–3 weeks — much faster than the paper era's 3–6 weeks.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which device-related step must be completed BEFORE test day?
o: Downloading Bluebook and completing the device check
questions.e: Download Bluebook ahead of time, run the device/exam setup check, and take a practice test in the app.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The lowest possible total SAT score is:
questions.e: 200 + 200 = 400 is the minimum total score; 1600 is the maximum.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which is a valid pacing target for Reading & Writing?
questions.e: 32 minutes ÷ 27 questions ≈ 1 minute 11 seconds each — bank time on quick questions for harder ones.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which is a valid pacing target for Math?
questions.e: 35 minutes ÷ 22 questions ≈ 1 minute 35 seconds each.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: If you miss several easy questions in Module 1, the most likely result is:
o: A harder Module 2 with bonus points
The easier Module 2 and a capped section score
questions.e: Module 1 accuracy drives routing; poor accuracy sends you to the easier Module 2, which caps your maximum section score.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The SAT is administered by:
questions.e: The College Board owns and administers the SAT (it contracts some operations, but the test is College Board's).

questions.subject: Overview

o: A strikethrough tool for eliminating choices
questions.e: Bluebook offers flagging, strikethrough, a calculator, and a reference sheet — but no spellchecker or grammar helper.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Students who need a testing device should request one from College Board at least:
questions.e: Students without a suitable device can borrow one from College Board if requested at least 30 days before test day.

questions.q: Which best describes the digital test's reading load per question?
o: One long passage shared by many questions

questions.e: Each R&W question has its own short passage (25–150 words) — you shift gears quickly between unrelated texts.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: A student scores 700 in Reading & Writing and 650 in Math. The total score is:
questions.e: Total = section scores added: 700 + 650 = 1350.

questions.e: The SAT reports each sitting's scores; many colleges then superscore by taking your best section scores across test dates.

o: Rest, eat a snack, use the restroom
questions.e: Use the break to reset: snack, water, restroom, stretch. You cannot start the next section early.

o: A valid photo ID matching the registration name
questions.e: Bring a valid photo ID (often a passport for international test takers) whose name matches your admission ticket.

questions.e: College Board provides six full-length adaptive practice tests in Bluebook — take at least two under timed conditions.

o: It is still offered alongside the digital test in the U.S.

questions.e: The SAT went fully digital internationally in 2023 and in the U.S. in spring 2024; the paper test is retired.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: The single biggest strategic implication of adaptive modules is:
o: Module 1 deserves your most careful work
You should skip hard Module 1 questions quickly
questions.e: Because Module 1 routes Module 2, careful accuracy on Module 1 — not rushing — protects your score ceiling.

questions.subject: Overview
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the Digital SAT's question presentation?
o: Long multi-page passages with many questions each
Short passages or single questions, one per screen
questions.e: The digital format uses short passages (25–150 words) with typically one question each — a major change from the old paper format.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q:
Biologist Amara Okafor spent three summers tracking pollinator visits to urban gardens. She found that gardens with at least five native flowering species attracted roughly twice as many bee visits per hour as gardens dominated by a single ornamental species. Okafor concluded that _____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: ornamental species are harmful to bees
plant diversity increases pollinator activity in urban gardens
bees prefer cities to rural areas
three summers is too short a study period
questions.e: The data compares diverse gardens vs. single-species gardens; the supported conclusion is that diversity increases visits. The other choices add claims the study never tested.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: The passage describes how 19th-century lighthouse keepers maintained meticulous logs of weather and ship traffic. The main idea is best summarized as:
o: Keepers' logs were an early form of systematic data collection
Ship traffic declined in the 19th century
questions.e: The passage's focus is the meticulous logging — a systematic record-keeping practice — not danger, decline, or weather alone.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The committee's report was thorough, yet its recommendations were never implemented." The word "yet" primarily signals:
o: A continuation of the same idea
A contrast between effort and outcome
questions.e: 'Yet' marks contrast: thorough report vs. unimplemented recommendations. This is an inference-about-relationship question in miniature.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Researchers played two recordings of birdsong to nesting sparrows: one from their own species, one from a distant species. The sparrows responded aggressively only to their own species' song. This suggests that sparrows:
o: Recognize and defend against same-species rivals
questions.e: Selective aggression toward their own species' song implies recognition of same-species rivals. 'Cannot hear' contradicts the differential response.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A student claims that library usage among teenagers has risen because of digital resources. Which evidence would most effectively support this claim?
o: A quotation from a librarian about loving books
Statistics showing ebook checkouts by teens doubling while print checkouts held steady
The number of libraries built last year
A teen saying libraries are quiet
questions.e: Command of evidence requires data matching the claim: rising teen usage driven by digital resources = ebook checkout statistics by teens.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Text: "Maya's grandmother spoke three languages, yet Maya grew up hearing only one. The family's move had silenced two tongues." What can be inferred?
o: Maya's grandmother refused to teach her
Migration reduced the family's language use
Three languages are too many to learn
questions.e: The move 'silenced two tongues' — the inference supported by the text is that migration reduced language use, not refusal or dislike.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A graph shows average test scores rising as study-group size falls from 8 to 3, then dropping when groups shrink to 2. The best-supported conclusion:
o: Groups of 3 outperformed both larger and smaller groups
Study groups do not affect scores
questions.e: Quantitative evidence: the peak is at 3 — better than 8 and better than 2. 'Always better' is contradicted by the drop at 2.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "Despite the drought, the orchard produced a record harvest." The sentence implies the harvest was:
questions.e: 'Despite' frames the record harvest as unexpected given the drought — a surprising outcome.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: An author argues that cities should plant more street trees, citing a study linking tree cover to lower summer temperatures. A critic would most weaken this argument by showing that:
o: The study's cooler neighborhoods also had more parks and reflective roofs
questions.e: An alternative cause (parks, reflective roofs) for the cooling weakens the claim that trees caused it — classic weaken-the-argument logic.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Passage: coral reefs bleached after a marine heatwave; reefs near upwelling zones recovered faster. The central idea:
o: Upwelling zones helped reefs recover from bleaching
questions.e: The contrast is recovery speed near upwelling zones — that is the passage's point, not rarity of heatwaves.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The historian argued that the railway did not merely connect cities; it reorganized time itself." The claim suggests the railway:
o: Changed how people experienced schedules and distance
questions.e: 'Reorganized time itself' = changed the experience of schedules and distance — an inference about the claim's meaning.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Which choice provides the strongest textual evidence that the character felt regret?
o: "She replayed the conversation nightly, wishing she had spoken."
questions.e: Only the replaying-and-wishing quotation directly evidences regret; the others are neutral actions.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A table shows Plant A grew 12 cm with fertilizer X and 7 cm without; Plant B grew 9 cm with X and 8 cm without. The data best support:
o: Fertilizer X helps Plant A more than Plant B
questions.e: Plant A gained 5 cm from X vs. Plant B's 1 cm — the fertilizer's effect was larger for A. Read the numbers, not the narrative.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The mayor promised reform, but the budget told a different story." The sentence suggests:
questions.e: 'Told a different story' = the budget contradicted the promise — a contrast inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Scientists found that mice navigating a maze with landmarks learned routes 40% faster than mice in a featureless maze. The finding supports the idea that:
questions.e: The 40% faster learning with landmarks directly supports landmarks aiding navigation — match the data to the claim.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A passage states that honeybee colonies with diverse gut microbes survived pesticide exposure better. The main idea is:
o: Microbial diversity may protect bees from pesticides
questions.e: The comparison (diverse microbes → better survival) supports a protective role; 'may' keeps it appropriately cautious.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "After the merger, the two rivals' logos — once displayed on opposite ends of the stadium — appeared side by side." The detail primarily illustrates:
o: The new unity of the merged companies
questions.e: Logos side by side after a merger illustrates corporate unity — the detail serves the merger narrative.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Which finding would most strengthen the claim that sleep improves memory?
o: Students who slept 8 hours recalled 25% more word pairs than those who slept 4 hours
questions.e: Strengthening requires a direct sleep–memory link: more sleep → better recall. Preferences and caffeine are irrelevant.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Text: "The novel's hero is fearless in battle but trembles when writing a letter home." This contrast suggests the hero:
o: Fears emotional vulnerability more than physical danger
questions.e: Fearless in battle yet trembling at a letter = emotional vulnerability outweighs physical danger — the supported inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A bar chart shows bus ridership rising 15% after fares were cut, while train ridership stayed flat. The best-supported claim:
questions.e: Only the bus change aligns with the fare cut; train ridership was flat, so 'all transit' is too broad.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The scientist's hypothesis was elegant, but the data were stubborn." The sentence implies:
o: The data did not fit the hypothesis
questions.e: 'Stubborn' data vs. an 'elegant' hypothesis = the data resisted fitting — contrast inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: An article claims electric scooters reduced downtown car trips, citing a 12% drop in parking revenue after scooters launched. The argument is weakened most by:
o: A new downtown parking garage with free parking opened the same month
questions.e: The free-parking garage offers an alternative explanation for the revenue drop — the classic confound that weakens causal claims.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Passage: two ancient cities had identical aqueduct designs; one thrived, one collapsed. Archaeologists attribute the difference to maintenance records showing regular repairs in the thriving city. The point:
o: Aqueduct design determines a city's fate
Maintenance, not design, explained the different outcomes
questions.e: Same design + different outcomes + maintenance records → maintenance explains the difference. Follow the controlled comparison.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "She had rehearsed the speech a dozen times, so the tremor in her voice surprised everyone." The tremor was surprising because:
o: Extensive rehearsal created an expectation of confidence
questions.e: The 'so' sets up expectation: a dozen rehearsals → confidence; the tremor violated it — hence surprise.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Which quotation best supports the claim that the town embraced the festival?
o: "Shops closed early and streets filled with music."
questions.e: Closed shops and filled streets show enthusiastic participation; duration, rain, and founding date do not evidence embrace.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Data: students using flashcards scored no better than those rereading notes, but students doing practice tests outperformed both. Conclusion:
o: Practice testing was the most effective method studied
questions.e: Practice testing outperformed both alternatives — it was the most effective of the three methods tested.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The new bridge halved commute times, yet traffic on the old road barely fell." The most logical inference:
o: New drivers filled the freed capacity on the old road
questions.e: If the bridge halved commutes yet old-road traffic barely fell, new demand must have replaced diverted drivers — induced demand.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A researcher claims urban green space lowers stress, showing lower cortisol in park visitors vs. shoppers. The claim needs which assumption?
o: The two groups were otherwise comparable
questions.e: Causal claims from group comparisons assume the groups were comparable — otherwise some other difference explains the cortisol gap.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Text: "The orchestra tuned for ten minutes; the audience's chatter faded as the first violinist raised her bow." The detail about chatter fading suggests:
questions.e: Fading chatter as the bow rises = the audience's attention shifting to anticipation — the natural inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Two studies of the same drug disagreed. Study A used 50 patients; Study B used 5,000 and found no effect. The disagreement most likely reflects:
o: Study B's larger sample giving a more reliable result
questions.e: Larger samples yield more reliable estimates; a 5,000-patient null result outweighs a 50-patient positive — sample size matters.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The chef tasted the soup, added salt, tasted again, and smiled." The sequence implies:
questions.e: Taste → adjust → taste → smile = the fix worked. Follow the sequence to the inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A line graph shows ice-cream sales and drowning incidents rising together each summer. The best-supported statement:
o: Both rise with warmer weather, a shared seasonal factor
questions.e: Correlation ≠ causation: summer heat drives both. Never pick a causal claim from correlational data alone.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The museum's new wing was funded entirely by small donations, a fact the director repeated at every gala." The director likely repeated it to:
questions.e: Repeating 'entirely by small donations' spotlights community-wide backing — the rhetorical purpose of the detail.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Passage: bilingual children switched languages mid-sentence when a word was missing, then continued fluently. Researchers concluded code-switching is:
questions.e: Switching to fill a gap and continuing fluently = strategic, not confused — the behavior matches the conclusion.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Which evidence best supports "the policy reduced accidents"?
o: Accidents fell 30% in the year after the policy began, with traffic volume unchanged
questions.e: A 30% drop with traffic volume held constant isolates the policy's effect — the 'unchanged' control is what makes it evidence.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "He kept the letter for twenty years, though he never answered it." The sentence suggests the letter:
questions.e: Keeping an unanswered letter for decades implies it mattered in an unresolved way — the supported inference.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: A survey finds 80% of gym members exercise mainly for mental health. The finding best supports:
o: Motivation for exercise is often psychological rather than physical
questions.e: 80% citing mental health = psychological motivation dominates — stay inside what the number actually says.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Text: "The lighthouse beam swept the cove every twelve seconds, and the smugglers timed their rowing to its rhythm." The smugglers' behavior shows:
questions.e: Timing rowing to the beam's rhythm = exploiting predictability — the inference the detail supports.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: Researchers compared test scores of students randomly assigned to quiet vs. noisy rooms; the quiet group scored 12% higher. The random assignment mainly ensures:
o: Pre-existing differences between groups were balanced
questions.e: Random assignment balances confounds across groups, letting the noise difference explain the score gap — experimental design logic.

questions.subject: Info & Ideas
questions.q: "The vineyard's oldest vines produced the fewest grapes but the most prized wine." The contrast implies:
questions.e: Fewest grapes yet most prized wine = quality diverging from quantity — the point of the contrast.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The scientist's argument was tenuous, resting on a single unverified observation." As used here, "tenuous" most nearly means:
questions.e: The clue 'resting on a single unverified observation' predicts 'weak/flimsy' — tenuous means thin or weak. Predict from the clue, then match.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A passage describes a character who collects broken clocks "not to repair them, but to remember that time, too, can stop." The detail about the clocks primarily serves to:
o: Show the character is a skilled repairman
Illustrate the character's reflective view of time
questions.e: Purpose questions ask about function: the 'not to repair but to remember' framing makes the clocks illustrate reflection on time.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A praises urban beekeeping as ecological restoration. Text B warns that city hives spread disease to wild pollinators. The two texts are best described as:
o: Presenting opposing views on urban beekeeping
questions.e: Cross-text: A is pro, B raises a counter-risk — opposing views on the same practice. Identify each claim, then the relationship.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The committee's decision was unanimous; not a single member dissented." The second clause functions as:
questions.e: 'Not a single member dissented' restates unanimous — the SAT plants such clues; use them to confirm word meaning.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: An author opens with a childhood memory, then presents statistics, then ends with a policy proposal. The structure is best described as:
questions.e: Text structure: personal story introduces, data supports, proposal concludes — anecdote, evidence, argument.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "Her prolific output — twelve novels in a decade — astonished critics." "Prolific" most nearly means:
questions.e: The dash-enclosed clue 'twelve novels in a decade' predicts 'productive' — prolific means producing abundantly.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Two historians discuss the same treaty: one calls it visionary, the other calls it reckless. A question asks how the second historian would respond to the first. The correct approach is to:
o: Identify the contrast in evaluation and select the choice reflecting disagreement
questions.e: Cross-text response questions: map each author's stance (visionary vs. reckless), then choose the response reflecting that disagreement.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The austere laboratory — bare walls, single bulb — reflected the team's focus." "Austere" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Bare walls, single bulb' predicts 'severely simple/plain' — austere means without decoration.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A paragraph lists three failed experiments before describing the successful one. The failed experiments primarily function to:
o: Establish the difficulty overcome by the success
questions.e: Function: failures before success establish difficulty and make the breakthrough meaningful — a common structure move.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "His apology was perfunctory, delivered without looking up from his phone." "Perfunctory" most nearly means:
questions.e: The clue 'without looking up from his phone' predicts 'half-hearted/minimal-effort' — perfunctory means done as a routine duty.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A argues desalination is too energy-intensive; Text B describes a new low-energy desalination membrane. Text B most likely:
o: Qualifies or challenges Text A's objection
questions.e: B's low-energy membrane answers A's energy objection — it challenges/qualifies the criticism rather than agreeing.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The volatile market swung wildly after the announcement." "Volatile" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Swung wildly' predicts 'unstable' — volatile means liable to rapid change.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: An author describes a glacier as "a slow river of ice." The comparison primarily serves to:
o: Make an abstract process vivid and understandable
questions.e: The metaphor's function is explanatory vividness — making slow ice movement graspable, not literal classification.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The witness's candid testimony — blunt, unrehearsed — surprised the court." "Candid" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Blunt, unrehearsed' predicts 'frank/open' — candid means truthful and straightforward.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Both texts discuss remote work. Text A cites productivity gains; Text B cites loneliness. A synthesis question asks what they agree on. The best answer would note:
o: That remote work has significant effects on workers
That remote work should be banned
questions.e: Despite opposite evaluations, both agree remote work significantly affects workers — find the shared premise beneath disagreement.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The pragmatic mayor focused on potholes rather than grand visions." "Pragmatic" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Focused on potholes rather than grand visions' predicts 'practical' — pragmatic means dealing with problems realistically.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A passage ends: "And so the lighthouse, built to warn ships away, became the very thing that drew them in." The ending primarily:
questions.e: Warning → attraction is an ironic reversal; endings that flip the opening image signal irony or paradox.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "Her meticulous notes — every measurement dated and initialed — impressed the auditors." "Meticulous" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Every measurement dated and initialed' predicts 'extremely careful' — meticulous means showing great attention to detail.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A: "Recycling programs cut landfill waste 30%." Text B: "Most recycled plastic is never actually reprocessed." The relationship is:
questions.e: B's 'never actually reprocessed' complicates A's success story — a qualifying counterpoint, not full agreement.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The obsolete machinery, untouched for decades, was finally scrapped." "Obsolete" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Untouched for decades' predicts 'no longer in use' — obsolete means out of date, disused.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: An author asks, "What if the cure is worse than the disease?" The rhetorical question primarily functions to:
o: Prompt readers to reconsider the proposed solution
questions.e: Rhetorical questions function to provoke reconsideration — here, doubting whether the remedy's costs exceed its benefits.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The resilient town rebuilt within a year of the flood." "Resilient" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Rebuilt within a year' predicts 'able to recover' — resilient means recovering quickly from difficulty.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A scientist's memoir moves from lab anecdotes to reflections on ethics. The shift primarily serves to:
o: Broaden the focus from personal story to larger questions
questions.e: Structure: anecdote → ethical reflection broadens scope from the personal to the universal — a standard move.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "His ambiguous reply — 'we'll see' — settled nothing." "Ambiguous" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'We'll see' + 'settled nothing' predicts 'unclear/open to interpretation' — ambiguous means having more than one meaning.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A claims AI tutors help struggling students; Text B shows AI tutors widening gaps between strong and weak students. The texts:
o: Reach different conclusions about AI tutors' effects
questions.e: Help vs. widen gaps = different conclusions about the same intervention. Map each claim before relating them.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The frugal traveler cooked every meal rather than dining out." "Frugal" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Cooked every meal rather than dining out' predicts 'economical/thrifty' — frugal means sparing with money.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A passage about bees begins with hive statistics, then zooms into a single forager's journey. This movement is best described as:
questions.e: Statistics (general) → one bee's journey (specific): the classic general-to-specific zoom.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The innovative design — unlike anything on the market — won the award." "Innovative" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Unlike anything on the market' predicts 'new/original' — innovative means featuring new ideas.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: An editorial compares a city's budget to a household budget. The comparison's purpose is to:
o: Make fiscal policy accessible through analogy
questions.e: Analogies function to clarify: the familiar household budget makes abstract fiscal policy concrete.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The diplomat's tactful phrasing avoided offending either side." "Tactful" most nearly means:
o: showing sensitivity in dealing with others
questions.e: 'Avoided offending either side' predicts 'diplomatic/sensitive' — tactful means skilled in handling delicate matters.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A describes coral restoration success; Text B describes coral restoration success at higher cost. The texts differ in:
questions.e: Same topic and outcome, different cost assessment — precision about the axis of difference matters in cross-text questions.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The stagnant pond, with no inflow for months, bred mosquitoes." "Stagnant" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'No inflow for months' predicts 'not moving' — stagnant means showing no activity or movement.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: A biography opens with the subject's most famous failure rather than birth. The likely purpose is to:
o: Hook readers with a striking, counterintuitive entry point
questions.e: Opening with failure is a hook: it surprises and promises an arc of recovery — structure serving engagement.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "Her vivid description — colors, sounds, smells — transported listeners." "Vivid" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Colors, sounds, smells' + 'transported listeners' predicts 'producing strong clear images' — vivid means intensely clear.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Two reviews of the same film: one praises its pacing, the other calls it rushed. They disagree about:
questions.e: Praised pacing vs. rushed = direct disagreement about pacing. Name the exact point of contention.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The controversial policy — debated for months in every forum — finally passed." "Controversial" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Debated for months in every forum' predicts 'causing disagreement' — controversial means giving rise to dispute.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: An author lists three objections to a plan, then answers each. The structure is:
questions.e: Objections followed by answers = objection-and-rebuttal, a standard argumentative structure.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The humble beginnings — a garage, two laptops — belied the company's ambition." "Humble" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'A garage, two laptops' predicts 'modest/unpretentious' — humble means low in rank or modest.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: Text A: "The policy succeeded." Text B: "The policy succeeded, but only for wealthy districts." Text B:
questions.e: 'But only for wealthy districts' narrows the success — a qualification, not a contradiction.

questions.subject: Craft & Structure
questions.q: "The inevitable result — given the drought and debt — was foreclosure." "Inevitable" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Given the drought and debt' predicts 'certain/unavoidable' — inevitable means certain to happen.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The new library is popular. _____, it closes at 6 p.m., frustrating evening studiers. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Popularity vs. early closing is a contrast — 'however' marks it. 'Moreover' would continue the same direction.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The storm knocked out power. _____, the hospital switched to generators. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Power loss → generator use is cause-effect — 'as a result' fits. Determine the relationship before reading choices.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: She studied daily. _____, she reviewed her error log weekly. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Daily study + weekly review continue the same idea — 'moreover' (continuation). Contrast words would reverse direction wrongly.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Many birds migrate. _____, the Arctic tern flies 70,000 km yearly. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: The tern is an example of migrating birds — 'for example' marks exemplification.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: He missed the bus. _____, he arrived late to the interview. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Missed bus → late arrival is cause-effect — 'consequently' fits.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The plan was expensive. _____, the council approved it unanimously. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Expensive yet approved = contrast — 'nevertheless' marks concession. 'Therefore' would wrongly imply the cost caused approval.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Choices include both "however" and "nevertheless" for a contrast blank. The best strategy is to:
o: Eliminate both, since two correct answers cannot exist
questions.e: Same-category transitions function identically; both cannot be right, so eliminate both and look elsewhere.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
While researching a topic, a student took these notes:
• Octopuses have three hearts.
• Two hearts stop beating when an octopus swims.
• The student wants to emphasize an unusual physiological trait.
Which choice best achieves the goal?
o: Octopuses are marine animals with eight arms.
Two of an octopus's three hearts stop beating while it swims.
questions.e: Rhetorical synthesis: match the goal (unusual trait) — only the hearts-stopping fact is unusual, and it is verified in the notes.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The soil was rich. _____, the harvest failed. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Rich soil vs. failed harvest = contrast — 'however'. Cause-effect words would claim the soil caused the failure.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Regular exercise improves sleep. _____, it strengthens the heart. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Two benefits continuing the same direction — 'in addition' (continuation).

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889.
• It was initially criticized by artists.
• The student wants to introduce the tower's controversial debut.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: The Eiffel Tower, built in 1889, faced criticism from artists at its debut.
The Eiffel Tower is in Paris.
questions.e: 'Controversial debut' = built in 1889 + criticized by artists — the choice combining both facts matches the goal exactly.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: He saved for months. _____, he could not afford the laptop. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Saving yet still unable = contrast — 'however' marks the frustrated expectation.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The data were flawed. _____, the conclusion was unreliable. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Flawed data → unreliable conclusion is cause-effect — 'thus' fits.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: She speaks three languages. _____, her brother speaks five. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Both siblings multilingual — the second continues/compares with the first: 'similarly' marks the parallel.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• Honeybees communicate through dances.
• The waggle dance indicates direction and distance.
• The student wants to explain how bees share location information.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: Through the waggle dance, honeybees communicate the direction and distance of food sources.
questions.e: The goal (how location info is shared) is met only by the waggle-dance choice, with both facts verified in the notes.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The museum is free on Sundays. _____, crowds are large. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Free admission → large crowds is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: He is a talented pianist. _____, he cannot read music. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Talented yet unable to read music = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: To answer a transitions question correctly, the first step should be:
o: Determine the logical relationship between the ideas
questions.e: Relationship first, choices second: identify contrast/cause/continuation, then match the word. Choices-first reading invites traps.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• Photosynthesis converts sunlight to energy.
• Chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue and red light.
• The student wants to explain why leaves are green.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light, reflecting green.
questions.e: 'Why leaves are green' requires the absorption + reflection logic — only the first choice uses the notes to explain the color.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The road was closed. _____, drivers took a detour. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Closure → detour is cause-effect — 'therefore' fits.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The first experiment failed. _____, the second succeeded brilliantly. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Failure vs. brilliant success = direct contrast — 'in contrast'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: She woke early. _____, she missed the train. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Waking early yet missing the train = contrast/concession — 'nevertheless'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• The Great Wall stretches over 21,000 km.
• It was built across many dynasties.
• The student wants to emphasize the wall's scale and long construction history.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: The Great Wall is in China.
Built across many dynasties, the Great Wall stretches over 21,000 km.
questions.e: The goal names two facts (scale + long history); only the choice containing both matches the goal.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Prices rose sharply. _____, demand remained strong. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Rising prices with strong demand defies expectation — 'surprisingly' marks the unexpected continuation.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The instructions were unclear. _____, most students completed the task. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Unclear instructions yet completion = concession — 'despite this' marks it.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: In rhetorical synthesis, if two answer choices are both factually correct, you should choose the one that:
o: Most directly achieves the stated goal
questions.e: Facts are necessary but not sufficient: the winner is the choice that accomplishes exactly what the question asks.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: He trained for a year. _____, he won the championship. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Training → victory is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The old bridge was narrow. _____, the new bridge has six lanes. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Narrow vs. six lanes = direct contrast — 'in contrast'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors.
• Adenosine promotes sleepiness.
• The student wants to explain why caffeine keeps people awake.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: By blocking adenosine receptors, caffeine prevents the sleepiness adenosine would promote.
questions.e: The mechanism (blocking receptors → preventing sleepiness) answers 'why' using both notes — goal matched, facts verified.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The lecture was long. _____, it was fascinating. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Long yet fascinating = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: She forgot her umbrella. _____, she got soaked. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: No umbrella → soaked is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: A transition sits between two sentences describing similar trends. The relationship is most likely:
questions.e: Similar trends continue the same direction — continuation transitions (moreover, similarly, in addition) fit.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• Volcanoes release ash that can cool the climate.
• The 1815 Tambora eruption caused the 'Year Without a Summer.'
• The student wants to give an example of volcanic cooling.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: The 1815 Tambora eruption, which caused the 'Year Without a Summer,' exemplifies how volcanic ash can cool the climate.
questions.e: 'Give an example of volcanic cooling' = the Tambora case linked to the general claim — the only choice doing both.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The team lost its star player. _____, morale stayed high. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Lost star yet high morale = concession — 'nevertheless'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: He apologized sincerely. _____, she forgave him. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Sincere apology → forgiveness is cause-effect — 'consequently'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Which pair of transitions belongs to the SAME category?
questions.e: 'Moreover' and 'furthermore' are both continuation/addition transitions; the other pairs mix categories.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q:
Notes:
• Glass frogs have translucent skin.
• Their organs are visible from below.
• The student wants to describe the frogs' distinctive appearance.
Which choice best achieves this?
o: Glass frogs' translucent skin reveals their organs from below, giving them a distinctive see-through appearance.
questions.e: 'Distinctive appearance' = translucent skin + visible organs combined — matches the descriptive goal with verified facts.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The recipe was simple. _____, the dish was delicious. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Simple yet delicious = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: Attendance doubled. _____, the organizers added a second session. Which transition best fits?
questions.e: Doubled attendance → second session is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Expression of Ideas
questions.q: The most common trap in rhetorical synthesis questions is a choice that is:
o: Factually true but does not achieve the stated goal
questions.e: True-but-off-goal choices are the signature trap: every fact checks out, but the choice answers a different question.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The team of researchers ___ submitted its findings yesterday.
questions.e: 'Team' is a collective noun treated as singular here ('its findings') — use 'has'. Ignore the plural 'researchers' inside the prepositional phrase.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Neither the manager nor the employees ___ aware of the change.
questions.e: With 'neither/nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'employees' is plural, so 'were'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The book, along with several articles, ___ on the reading list.
questions.e: Phrases like 'along with' do not change the subject's number: 'book' is singular — 'is'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She ___ in this city since 2015.
questions.e: 'Since 2015' signals an action continuing to the present — present perfect 'has lived'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q:
Running down the street, ___.

Which ending avoids a dangling modifier?
questions.e: The participial phrase 'running down the street' must modify the subject — 'she' is the one running. The other subjects cannot run.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The experiment was a success ___ the results confirmed the hypothesis.
questions.e: Two independent clauses can be joined by a period, semicolon, or comma+conjunction. A bare comma would be a comma splice — but a dash is not offered, so all listed options work.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Each of the students ___ a laptop.
questions.e: 'Each' is singular — 'each of the students has'. Do not let the plural 'students' mislead you.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The data ___ conclusive.
questions.e: 'Data' is plural (singular: datum) — 'are conclusive'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Between you and ___, the test was easy.
questions.e: Objects of prepositions take objective case: 'between you and me'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The committee will announce ___ decision tomorrow.
questions.e: 'Its' = possessive; 'it's' = 'it is'. The committee's decision → 'its decision'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: By the time we arrived, the movie ___.
questions.e: Past perfect 'had started' marks the earlier of two past events (movie started before we arrived).

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The reason for the delay was ___ the bridge was closed.
questions.e: 'The reason ... was that ...' — 'because' after 'the reason' is redundant ('the reason because' is nonstandard).

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She is one of the players who ___ selected for the finals.
questions.e: The relative clause modifies 'players' (plural): 'players who were selected'. 'One of the players' sets up a plural antecedent.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The manager asked the team to complete the report ___ Friday.
questions.e: 'By Friday' = no later than Friday. 'Until Friday' would mean continuously up to Friday — wrong for a deadline.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Neither of the answers ___ correct.
questions.e: 'Neither' is singular — 'neither of the answers is correct'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The ancient manuscript, ___ pages were brittle, was carefully preserved.
questions.e: 'Whose' = possessive relative pronoun for the manuscript's pages. 'Who's' = 'who is'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: He has been working here ___ five years.
questions.e: 'For' + duration (five years); 'since' + starting point (2019).

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The results of the survey ___ published yesterday.
questions.e: Subject is 'results' (plural) — 'were published'. Ignore the singular-sounding prepositional phrase.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: ___ going to the store, she bought milk.
questions.e: 'While she was going' — the clause needs a subject ('she'). 'While going' alone would dangle.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The number of applicants ___ increased this year.
questions.e: 'The number' is singular — 'has increased'. Contrast: 'a number of applicants have' (plural).

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She gave the book to ___.
questions.e: Objects of the preposition 'to' take objective case: 'him and me'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The scientist, along with her assistants, ___ conducting the experiment.
questions.e: 'Along with her assistants' is parenthetical — the subject 'scientist' is singular: 'is'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: He did not know ___ to solve the problem.
questions.e: 'How to solve' — the idiom is 'know how to', not 'know what to solve' here.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The cake was divided ___ the four children.
questions.e: 'Among' for three or more; 'between' for two. Four children → 'among'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She is taller than ___.
questions.e: Elliptical comparison: 'taller than I (am)'. Formal standard English uses subject case after 'than'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The committee ___ divided on the issue.
questions.e: Here the members act individually ('divided'), so the collective noun takes a plural verb: 'are'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q:
Having finished the report, ___.

Which ending is correct?
questions.e: 'Having finished' must modify 'she' — she is the one who finished. Other subjects dangle.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Either the teacher or the students ___ responsible.
questions.e: 'Either/or': verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'students' → 'are'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The museum's new exhibit, ___ opens Friday, features local artists.
questions.e: Nonrestrictive clause (set off by commas) requires 'which', not 'that'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: He speaks English ___.
questions.e: Adverb 'well' modifies the verb 'speaks'; 'good' is an adjective.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The news ___ surprising.
questions.e: 'News' is singular despite the -s ending — 'was surprising'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She will graduate ___ June.
questions.e: Months take 'in' (in June); specific days take 'on' (on June 5).

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The dog wagged ___ tail.
questions.e: Possessive 'its' — no apostrophe. 'It's' always means 'it is'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Not only the students but also the teacher ___ excited.
questions.e: 'Not only/but also': verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'teacher' → 'was'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The professor asked that each student ___ the form.
questions.e: Subjunctive after 'asked that': base form 'complete', not 'completes'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: There ___ many reasons for the delay.
questions.e: 'There are' — the true subject 'reasons' is plural. Invert mentally: 'many reasons are there'.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: She bought three ___.
questions.e: Plural of tomato = 'tomatoes'. Apostrophes never form simple plurals.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: He is capable ___ solving difficult problems.
questions.e: Idiom: 'capable of' + gerund. 'Capable to solve' is nonstandard.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: The children enjoyed ___ in the park.
questions.e: "Enjoyed" is reflexive here: the children perform the enjoyment on themselves, so the reflexive pronoun "themselves" is required.

questions.subject: Conventions
questions.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.e: Two independent clauses: semicolon works; bare comma = comma splice; no punctuation = run-on; colon misused here.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The candid review — honest to a fault — cost him the endorsement." "Candid" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Honest to a fault' is the clue — candid means frank and straightforward. Predict from the clue, then match.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The town was quiet. _____, the festival drew thousands. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Quiet town vs. thousands of visitors = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "Her lucid explanation — clear and step-by-step — helped everyone." "Lucid" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Clear and step-by-step' predicts 'clear/easy to understand' — lucid means expressed clearly.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: He exercised daily. _____, his health improved. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Exercise → improved health is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms — gone in a week — draws crowds." "Ephemeral" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Gone in a week' predicts 'short-lived' — ephemeral means lasting a very short time.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: She saved money. _____, she invested wisely. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Saving + investing continue the same prudent direction — 'in addition'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The versatile tool — useful for cutting, measuring, and prying — was a favorite." "Versatile" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Useful for cutting, measuring, and prying' predicts 'adaptable to many uses' — versatile means able to do many things.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The evidence was weak. _____, the jury acquitted. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Weak evidence yet acquittal = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "His reluctant agreement — given only after hours of debate — surprised no one." "Reluctant" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Given only after hours of debate' predicts 'unwilling/hesitant' — reluctant means unwilling.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: Temperatures dropped. _____, the lake froze. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Cold → freezing is cause-effect — 'consequently'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The meticulous archive — every document labeled — aided researchers." "Meticulous" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Every document labeled' predicts 'extremely careful' — meticulous means showing great attention to detail.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: He is generous. _____, his sister is equally kind. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Parallel traits — 'similarly' marks the comparison.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The ambiguous instructions — open to several readings — confused the team." "Ambiguous" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Open to several readings' predicts 'unclear' — ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The store was crowded. _____, service was fast. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Crowded yet fast = concession — 'nevertheless'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The pragmatic solution — cheap and quick — was adopted." "Pragmatic" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Cheap and quick' predicts 'practical' — pragmatic means dealing with problems in a practical way.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: She studied art. _____, she learned sculpture. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Sculpture is an example within art study — 'for example' marks exemplification.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The formidable opponent — undefeated in ten bouts — intimidated newcomers." "Formidable" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Undefeated in ten bouts' + 'intimidated' predicts 'inspiring fear' — formidable means arousing fear or respect through power.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The rain stopped. _____, the match resumed. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Rain stopping → resuming is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The innovative method — never tried before — doubled yields." "Innovative" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Never tried before' predicts 'new/original' — innovative means introducing new ideas.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The book was long. _____, it was gripping. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Long yet gripping = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The tedious lecture — three hours of monotone — emptied the hall." "Tedious" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Three hours of monotone' + 'emptied the hall' predicts 'boring' — tedious means too long and tiresome.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: He missed practice. _____, the coach benched him. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Missed practice → benched is cause-effect — 'thus'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "Her frugal habits — mending clothes, cooking at home — built savings." "Frugal" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Mending clothes, cooking at home' predicts 'thrifty' — frugal means careful with money.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The first dish was spicy. _____, the second was mild. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Spicy vs. mild = direct contrast — 'in contrast'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The vivid mural — bright colors covering the wall — stopped passersby." "Vivid" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Bright colors' predicts 'strikingly bright/clear' — vivid means producing powerful, clear images.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: She woke late. _____, she caught the bus. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Late yet caught the bus = concession — 'nevertheless'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The resilient reef — recovering after bleaching — amazed divers." "Resilient" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Recovering after bleaching' predicts 'able to recover' — resilient means recovering quickly.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: He loves coffee. _____, he drinks three cups daily. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Three cups daily exemplifies loving coffee — 'for instance'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The controversial decision — protested by hundreds — was reversed." "Controversial" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Protested by hundreds' predicts 'causing dispute' — controversial means giving rise to public disagreement.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The path was steep. _____, the view was worth it. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Steep yet worth it = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The humble cottage — small and plain — suited the writer." "Humble" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Small and plain' predicts 'modest' — humble means of modest nature.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: Prices fell. _____, sales surged. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Falling prices → surging sales is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The obsolete system — replaced years ago — was finally removed." "Obsolete" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Replaced years ago' predicts 'no longer used' — obsolete means no longer in use.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: She is a doctor. _____, her husband is a nurse. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Parallel medical professions — 'similarly' marks the comparison.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The stagnant air — motionless for hours — felt heavy." "Stagnant" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Motionless for hours' predicts 'not moving' — stagnant means showing no activity.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The movie was short. _____, it felt endless. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Short yet endless-feeling = contrast — 'however'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The austere chapel — bare stone, no decoration — impressed visitors." "Austere" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'Bare stone, no decoration' predicts 'severely plain' — austere means without decoration.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: He trained hard. _____, he broke the record. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Training → record is cause-effect — 'as a result'.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: "The tenuous link — one weak study — was widely criticized." "Tenuous" most nearly means:
questions.e: 'One weak study' predicts 'weak' — tenuous means thin or weak.

questions.subject: Vocab & Transitions
questions.q: The drought persisted. _____, reservoirs fell to record lows. Which transition fits?
questions.e: Persistent drought → falling reservoirs is cause-effect — 'consequently'.
